cards.title: pV = nRT: match the units to the pressure asked for

walkthrough.question:
A 3.0 dm³ cylinder holds 64 g of oxygen gas, O₂, at 25.0 °C. R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and PV = nRT. Which expression gives the pressure in pascals?
A. (2 × 8.31 × 25) / 3.0
B. (2 × 8.31 × 298) / (3.0 × 10⁻³)
C. (2 × 8.31 × 298) / 3.0
D. (4 × 8.31 × 298) / (3.0 × 10⁻³)
walkthrough.key_idea: Pascals need volume in m³, temperature in kelvin and n in moles.
walkthrough.question_type: Ideal gas equation: find a variable
walkthrough.careful: Check the pressure unit asked: dm³ gives kPa, m³ gives Pa.
procedure: Rearrange PV = nRT for the quantity asked.
Convert mass to moles using n = m/M.
Convert temperature to kelvin by adding 273.
Convert volume to m³ when pressure is in Pa.
Substitute, then check the unit of the answer.
tricks: dm³ pairs with kPa, m³ pairs with Pa. Fails if the units get mixed.
Scan options for a Celsius value first: it removes that option at once.
if_lost: Which unit does the question want the pressure in?
What units does each symbol in PV = nRT need?
What is the mass of one mole of O₂ molecules?
What is 1 dm³ in m³?

1_context.short: Core PV = nRT problem, testing units rather than algebra.
1_context.why: R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is built on Pa, m³, K and mol, so every input must match that set to give pascals.
1_context.avoid: Substituting the printed values without converting them.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.4: PV = nRT links pressure, volume, temperature and amount; SI units only.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books work examples in one tidy unit set. This question tests which unit set the requested pressure forces.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only B combines moles, kelvin and m³ to give pascals.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Each wrong option changes one input from the full SI set, so each one marks a single known slip.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Missing that Pa was asked, not kPa: the most common mistake (24N.1.HL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Correct numbers with V in dm³ give kPa, so option C misses the mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B and C differ only in the 10⁻³ on the volume.

3_novel_application.short: Looks like arithmetic, but the options differ only in inputs.
3_novel_application.why: The options are unevaluated expressions, so nothing needs calculating. Comparing them in pairs shows exactly which conversion is being tested.
3_novel_application.avoid: Working each expression out on a calculator.
3_novel_application.disguise: The answers are expressions, so the skill being tested is unit choice, not calculation.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask what changes between two options: each change names one conversion to check.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: choose one expression for one mark.
4_command_terms.why: Credit rests only on the letter, so effort belongs in choosing inputs, not in producing a number.
4_command_terms.avoid: Evaluating the expression to a final pressure.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the expression that gives the pressure in pascals.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing, for the correct letter.

5_time_efficiency.short: Check n, then T, then V, and stop.
5_time_efficiency.why: Each of the three checks removes an option, so the correct expression is left without using a calculator.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the arithmetic: only the expression is asked for.

6_data_booklet.short: Booklet gives the equation, R, kelvin and dm³ to m³.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 4 states temperature (K) = °C + 273.15 and 1 dm³ = 1 × 10⁻³ m³, so these are read, not recalled.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Recalling the volume conversion from memory under time pressure.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 1: PV = nRT and n = m/M. Section 2: R. Section 4: kelvin and dm³ to m³.
6_data_booklet.memorise: That R's units require m³ and Pa is NOT in the booklet as a rule; infer it from J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

7_elimination.short: A uses Celsius, C keeps dm³, D doubles the moles.
7_elimination.why: Each wrong option breaks one fixed rule, so all three fall without any calculation.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping A because 25 is the number printed in the question.

definitely_wrong.rule: 25 is a Celsius value; the gas equation needs kelvin.
Volume left in dm³ gives kPa, not the pascals requested.
4 mol treats O₂ as atoms; 64 g of O₂ is 2 mol.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.4: solve problems with PV = nRT; units of volume and pressure are SI only.
1_context.textbook_gap: Textbooks drill rearrangement. Exams test unit discipline and multi-stage setup: moles from mass or from an equation, then substitution, often without a calculator on Paper 1.

trigger_phrases: moles from mass ÷ molar mass first
pressure stated with its unit, such as kPa with V in dm³
trap_boundaries: Temperature left in Celsius: 16% chose this in 24N.1.SL.TZ0.4 and it recurs in 25M.2.SL.TZ1.5.
Volume unit wrong for pascals: more than half chose dm³ in 24N.1.SL.TZ0.4.
Mass used for n, and power-of-ten slips from volume units (24N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
Answer from m³ data not converted to the requested cm³ (12M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: In 24N.2.HL.TZ0.1 the first mark is moles and the second the substituted volume; a correct final answer earns both, within a stated range. In 19N.2.SL.TZ0.6 the mark needs (127 + 273) K in the working's result.

disguises: Molar mass of an unknown from gas density: rearranging was a reported struggle (24M.2.SL.TZ2.1).
Molar mass of butane from gas collected over water: mass lost, volume, pressure and temperature are all needed (17M.3.SL.TZ2.2).
Gas produced by a decomposition: count moles of gas from the equation first (19N.2.SL.TZ0.6).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Three of P, V, T and n known means PV = nRT. For molar mass, get n first, then M = m/n.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Calculate earns marks stage by stage, with full marks for a correct final answer where the markscheme says so (24N.2.HL.TZ0.1). MCQs are one mark for the letter.

workflow: Check unit asked at the end
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: On expression-style MCQs, skip the arithmetic. On written parts, skip long routes such as assuming STP when conditions are given (24M.2.SL.TZ2.4).

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 1 has PV = nRT and n = m/M, section 2 has R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, section 4 has the kelvin and dm³ conversions. 1 kPa = 1000 Pa does NOT appear in these sections: memorise it.

rules: Any expression using a Celsius value in T is wrong.
With V in dm³ and R = 8.31 the result is in kPa, so reject it if Pa is asked.
Check n against the formula: a diatomic gas's moles use its molecular mass.

evidence.note: Worked question, answer B; just over half correct, Pa versus kPa the commonest slip.
40% correct; over half chose dm³, 16% used Celsius.
Celsius, mass for n and power-of-ten volume errors.
2025 report: Celsius and mismatched pressure and volume units.
47.58% correct; 38.82% chose a Celsius option.
15.5% correct on gas law with temperature conversion.
Answer came out in m³ and was not converted to cm³.
PV = nRT users ran into unit problems with R in J.
Moles of gas from the equation, then pressure in kPa with V in dm³.
Moles then volume; two marks for correct final answer.
Butane molar mass practical: quantities needed; Celsius listed as a cause of a low value.
Struggles combining ideal gas and density equations.
Long-winded calculations assuming STP.

cards.difficulty_signal: Hardest in the pack: 14M.1.HL.TZ1.2 at 15.5%, 24N.1.SL.TZ0.4 at 40%, 13M.1.SL.TZ1.5 at 47.58%. Unit errors still reported in May 2025.

cards.title: Gas law ratios: kelvin first, then direct or inverse

walkthrough.question:
An ideal gas in a container of fixed volume starts at 30 °C with pressure P Pa. It is warmed to 60 °C. What is its pressure now, in Pa?
A. Half of P
B. A little less than P
C. A little more than P
D. Two times P
walkthrough.key_idea: Ratios use kelvin: 30 °C to 60 °C is only 303 K to 333 K.
walkthrough.question_type: Gas law ratio: one variable changes
walkthrough.careful: Convert Celsius to kelvin before forming any ratio.
procedure: Write the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
Cancel whatever stays constant.
Convert any temperatures to kelvin.
Find the ratio for the changing pair.
Scale the starting value by that ratio.
tricks: Doubling a Celsius value does not double kelvin, so never double the pressure.
P and T are direct; P and V are inverse. Fails if n changes.
Doubling volume halves pressure: that is a 50% fall, not 100%.
if_lost: Which quantities stay fixed in this container?
Does heating at fixed volume raise or lower the pressure?
Which temperature scale do gas laws need?
What are the two temperatures on that scale?

1_context.short: Fixed volume means pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature.
1_context.why: The combined gas law cancels V and n, leaving P/T constant. It holds only on an absolute scale, where zero means zero particle motion.
1_context.avoid: Treating Celsius numbers as proportional to pressure.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.3: investigate how temperature, pressure and volume relate for a fixed mass of ideal gas.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach the law with kelvin already given. Here Celsius values are chosen so the obvious doubling is wrong.

2_markscheme_logic.short: 333/303 is about 1.1, so slightly above P.
2_markscheme_logic.why: A 30 degree rise is small compared with about 300 K, so the change in pressure is only about 10%.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Doubling because 60 is twice 30: reported in 09N.1.HL.TZ0.4 and 08M.1.SL.TZ0.13.
trigger_phrases: P proportional to T at fixed V
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The Celsius ratio 60/30 leads to D, which earns nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D uses 60/30 in Celsius; C uses 333/303 in kelvin.

3_novel_application.short: Words replace numbers, but it is still a ratio.
3_novel_application.why: The options are descriptions, so only size and direction matter. Estimate the kelvin ratio and pick the option that matches.
3_novel_application.avoid: Hunting for a formula that gives a numerical pressure.
3_novel_application.disguise: No value of P is given, and the answers are verbal, so it feels like theory.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask two things: which way does P move, and is the kelvin change big or small?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: choose the matching description.
4_command_terms.why: Only direction and size decide this mark, so there is no working to show and no precision needed.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing out a full calculation to several figures.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the description matching the new pressure.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing, for the correct letter.

5_time_efficiency.short: Add 273, compare, and choose within 30 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Rounded kelvin values are enough because options are far apart, so no calculator or exact fraction is needed.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the exact value: only 'a little more' has to be recognised.

6_data_booklet.short: Sections 1 and 4 give the law and kelvin conversion.
6_data_booklet.why: The combined gas law and K = °C + 273.15 are both printed, so nothing about the route needs memorising.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Forgetting the printed conversion when the question gives only Celsius.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 1: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. Section 4: temperature (K) = temperature (°C) + 273.15.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Cancelling constants is your job: no booklet entry lists the direct and inverse pairs.

7_elimination.short: Heating cannot lower pressure; kelvin has not doubled.
7_elimination.why: At fixed volume, hotter particles hit the walls harder and more often, so pressure must rise; doubling needs about 606 K.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping D as the neat-looking answer.

definitely_wrong.rule: Heating at fixed volume cannot lower the pressure.
Heating at fixed volume cannot lower the pressure.
Doubling pressure needs doubled kelvin, which 30 °C to 60 °C is not.

walkthrough.answer: C. P₂ = P × 333/303 ≈ 1.1 P, so a little more than P.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.3: temperature, pressure and volume relationships for a fixed mass, including analysing graphs. Names of gas laws are not assessed.
1_context.textbook_gap: Textbooks name the laws; exams never need the names. They test proportional reasoning, and graphs whose temperature axis may be in Celsius or kelvin.

trigger_phrases: convert to kelvin before the ratio
direct with T, inverse with V
trap_boundaries: Doubling a Celsius value and doubling the answer: 08M.1.SL.TZ0.13 and 09N.1.HL.TZ0.4.
More candidates chose the unconverted value than the right one in 18N.1.HL.TZ0.2.
A graph showing zero gas volume at 0 °C is wrong, yet it was widely chosen (24M.1.HL.TZ2.39).
A pressure fall of 100% is impossible: halving is a 50% fall (25M.1A.HL.6207.17).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: The full answer scales by the kelvin ratio. The tempting answer scales by the printed Celsius ratio.

disguises: Choosing a graph with a Celsius or kelvin axis (24M.1.SL.TZ2.29).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Volume reaches zero only at 0 K. On a Celsius axis the same straight line does not pass through the origin.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ forms are one mark for the letter. Calculations and graphs need correct temperature scale and labelled axes for their credit.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not use PV = nRT with R when only a ratio is needed. 08M.1.SL.TZ0.13 needed just 300 to 330.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 1 prints the combined gas law; section 4 prints the kelvin conversion. Which pairs are direct or inverse is NOT listed: read it from the equation's form.

rules: Heating at fixed volume or fixed pressure can never decrease P or V respectively.
Doubling of pressure or volume from doubled Celsius is wrong unless the kelvin value doubles too.
A drop of 100% in pressure is impossible for a gas that is still present.
A V–T graph reaching zero at 0 °C is wrong.

evidence.note: Worked question, answer C.
Volume doubled at constant temperature: pressure falls 50%, answer D.
Hardest on the paper at 15.27%: doubled T and doubled V; 300 to 330 was enough.
Most thought doubling Celsius doubles pressure.
Most common answer was the one not converted to kelvin.
Many chose a graph showing zero gas volume at 0 °C.
Gas law graphs with different temperature units confused candidates.

cards.difficulty_signal: Repeatedly hardest on its paper: 08M.1.SL.TZ0.13 at 15.27%, 09N.1.HL.TZ0.4 at 28%. Tested again in November 2025.

cards.title: Real gases: conditions, forces and the correct cause

walkthrough.question:
Four rows pair a gas with a set of conditions. Which row shows the smallest departure from ideal gas behaviour?
A. Phosphine, PH₃: low pressure, high temperature
B. Ammonia, NH₃: low pressure, high temperature
C. Phosphine, PH₃: high pressure, low temperature
D. Ammonia, NH₃: high pressure, low temperature
walkthrough.key_idea: Most ideal: low pressure, high temperature, weakest intermolecular forces.
walkthrough.question_type: Real gases: identify most ideal conditions
walkthrough.careful: Fix the conditions first, then compare the gases' intermolecular forces.
procedure: Choose low pressure: particles far apart, volume negligible.
Choose high temperature: attractions matter less.
Identify the intermolecular forces in each remaining gas.
Choose the gas with the weaker forces.
tricks: Hydrogen bonding means less ideal. Fails if the conditions also differ between rows.
High pressure: particle volume matters. Low temperature: attractions matter.
if_lost: What does the ideal model assume about particle volume and forces?
Which pressure makes particle volume matter least?
Which temperature makes attractions matter least?
Which of these two molecules can hydrogen bond?

1_context.short: Tests both assumptions of the ideal model at once.
1_context.why: The model assumes negligible particle volume and no forces. Low pressure and high temperature make both nearly true; weak forces help further.
1_context.avoid: Judging only by conditions, which leaves two rows tied.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.2: real gases deviate from the model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list the conditions. This question adds a comparison between gases, which needs bonding knowledge.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Conditions remove two rows; hydrogen bonding separates the other two.
2_markscheme_logic.why: NH₃ molecules hydrogen bond; PH₃ molecules attract far more weakly. With identical conditions, weaker forces mean behaviour closer to ideal.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Stopping at the conditions and picking between the two gases by guesswork.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Right conditions with the hydrogen-bonded gas (B) still misses the mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A and B share conditions; only the intermolecular forces of the gas differ.

3_novel_application.short: A table hides two separate judgements: conditions, then gas.
3_novel_application.why: Treating each column separately turns a four-way choice into two yes-or-no decisions, each using knowledge you already have.
3_novel_application.avoid: Reading the table row by row as four unrelated facts.
3_novel_application.disguise: Two variables and two gases arranged in a table look like recall of a specific fact.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Fix conditions first, then ask which gas attracts itself least.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: choose one row.
4_command_terms.why: The mark is for the letter alone, so no explanation is needed even though the reasoning has two stages.
4_command_terms.avoid: Spending time ranking all four rows.
4_command_terms.demands: Identify the row with the least deviation.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing, for the correct letter.

5_time_efficiency.short: Cross off two rows, compare two gases, done.
5_time_efficiency.why: Conditions remove half the options in seconds, leaving a single intermolecular force comparison.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Estimating boiling points or sizes of the gases.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip molar mass and London force comparisons: hydrogen bonding decides this pair.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet section helps; this is reasoning from structure.
6_data_booklet.why: Deviation has no equation or table here. The syllabus states no mathematical coverage is required, so it rests on the model's assumptions.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for gas data during the question.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None: use the model's assumptions and the molecule's bonding.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: the ideal model's assumptions, the deviation conditions, and which molecules hydrogen bond.

7_elimination.short: High pressure with low temperature is never closest to ideal.
7_elimination.why: Those conditions crowd slow particles together, so particle volume and attractions both matter, the opposite of what the model assumes.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping C because phosphine has weak forces: bad conditions dominate here.

definitely_wrong.rule: High pressure and low temperature cause the most deviation.
Worst conditions, and the gas hydrogen bonds as well.
Same conditions as A, but ammonia has stronger forces through hydrogen bonding.

walkthrough.answer: A. Low pressure and high temperature bring any gas nearest to ideal, and PH₃ lacks the hydrogen bonding present in NH₃.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.1: the ideal model has negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions. S1.5.2: deviation at low temperature and high pressure; no maths required.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give one sentence on deviation. Exams ask which assumption fails and why, and they separate the volume cause from the force cause.

trigger_phrases: not behaving as an ideal gas / a real gas
trap_boundaries: A volume above the PV = nRT prediction at very high pressure comes from molecular volume. Intermolecular forces would not cause it (24N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
A true statement that does not explain the deviation does not earn credit: many chose it in 16M.1.HL.TZ0.3 and 16M.1.SL.TZ0.4.
Comparing gases needs both named forces and which is stronger (19N.2.SL.TZ0.6).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: In 24N.2.HL.TZ0.1 one mark is for the non-ideal behaviour and one for non-negligible molecular volume. In 19N.2.SL.TZ0.6, naming each gas's forces alone falls short of linking stronger forces in water to deviation.

disguises: Measured volume larger than calculated at very high pressure (24N.2.HL.TZ0.1).
N₂ and H₂O formed together: which deviates more? (19N.2.SL.TZ0.6)
Stating the assumption behind a gas volume result: both gases behave ideally (21M.2.SL.TZ1.2).
A question not stating 'ideal' may expect real forces (10M.1.SL.TZ1.14).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Bigger volume than predicted: particles take up space. Smaller volume than predicted: particles attract.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Marks come per point: state non-ideal behaviour, then give the cause. A true statement unrelated to the cause scores nothing extra.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No equations needed: the syllabus states no mathematical coverage of deviation.

6_data_booklet.hack: None of the gas sections help. The assumptions and deviation conditions are NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: High pressure with low temperature is never the closest to ideal.
If conditions match, a hydrogen-bonded gas is less ideal than a similar gas without it. Conditions decide first if they differ.
Intermolecular attraction cannot explain a volume larger than predicted.

evidence.note: Worked question, answer A.
Not ideal at very high pressure; molecular volume not negligible.
Most cited forces, which would not raise volume above prediction.
N₂ versus water: forces compared, water deviates through attraction.
19.64% correct; majority chose a true statement that was not an explanation.
13.77% correct; same distractor.
Few could distinguish the cause of real versus ideal differences.
Assumption mark: both gases behave as ideal gases.
Question not mentioning ideal gases: intermolecular forces in real gas accepted.

cards.difficulty_signal: 16M.1.SL.TZ0.4 at 13.77% and 16M.1.HL.TZ0.3 at 19.64%; flagged as difficult in the November 2024 and May 2024 reports.

cards.title: Molar volume: moles, mole ratio, then the volume unit

walkthrough.question:
Copper, 1.28 g, reacts completely with excess nitric acid: Cu(s) + 4HNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2NO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). At STP the molar volume of an ideal gas is 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹. What volume of nitrogen dioxide forms, in cm³, at STP?
A. 227
B. 456
C. 684
D. 914
walkthrough.key_idea: Moles of Cu, doubled for NO₂, times 22.7, then dm³ to cm³.
walkthrough.question_type: Molar volume: mass to gas volume
walkthrough.careful: Apply the mole ratio before multiplying by molar volume; check requested unit.
procedure: Find moles of the given substance using n = m/M.
Use the equation's ratio to get moles of gas.
Multiply by the molar volume at those conditions.
Convert to the unit the question asks.
tricks: At STP, each 227 cm³ is 0.01 mol: read the moles from options.
22.7 applies only at STP. Fails at other conditions: use PV = nRT.
Gases at same conditions: volume ratio equals mole ratio. Fails for solids and solutions.
if_lost: Which reactant runs out, given that the acid is in excess?
How many moles of copper are in 1.28 g?
How many NO₂ form per copper in the equation?
Is the molar volume in the same unit the answer needs?

1_context.short: STP plus a mass: molar volume replaces PV = nRT.
1_context.why: At fixed temperature and pressure all ideal gases have the same molar volume, so gas volume depends only on moles, whichever gas it is.
1_context.avoid: Setting up PV = nRT with R when STP is stated.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.3: molar volume of an ideal gas is constant at a given temperature and pressure; its STP value is in the booklet.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books practise gas alone. This question requires an equation, an excess reagent and a unit change together.

2_markscheme_logic.short: 0.0201 mol Cu gives 0.0403 mol NO₂, or 914 cm³.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Two NO₂ form per Cu, so moles double. Then 0.0403 × 22.7 = 0.914 dm³, and 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Dividing or multiplying by 2 wrongly even with a correct equation: reported in 12M.2.HL.TZ2.2.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Skipping the 2:1 ratio gives about 456 cm³, option B.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B stops at moles of Cu; D doubles for NO₂.

3_novel_application.short: Looks like redox, but it is just moles to volume.
3_novel_application.why: The nitric acid, nitrate and water are noise: excess acid means copper alone sets the amount of gas.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using the moles or volume of nitric acid.
3_novel_application.disguise: A long equation with an acid in excess looks harder than a mole conversion.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Find the single (g) product asked for, then link it to the given mass only.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one number decides the letter.
4_command_terms.why: The options are widely spaced, so a rough mole estimate is enough. No working is marked.
4_command_terms.avoid: Showing or chasing several significant figures.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the volume produced in cm³.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing, for the correct letter.

5_time_efficiency.short: Round Cu to 64, estimate 0.04 mol, spot 914.
5_time_efficiency.why: The options are near multiples of 0.01 mol at STP, so 0.04 mol points to the answer without a calculator.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Using a calculator to four figures on a Paper 1A estimate.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the acid and all aqueous products: only Cu and NO₂ matter.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 2 prints 22.7; section 4 prints STP and cm³.
6_data_booklet.why: Molar volume at STP is in section 2, the conditions and 1 dm³ = 1 × 10³ cm³ in section 4, so neither needs recalling.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Using an older molar volume value.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 1: n = m/M. Section 2: Vm = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ at STP. Section 4: STP is 273.15 K and 100 kPa.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Atomic mass of Cu is NOT in these sections; find it in the periodic table, and write the equation ratio yourself.

7_elimination.short: Rough 0.02 mol Cu leaves only 0.04 mol NO₂.
7_elimination.why: Each option maps to a mole count; only the count matching the 2:1 ratio survives, so the others need no exact calculation.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking B because its moles match copper's.

definitely_wrong.rule: It equals 0.01 mol, halving copper's moles rather than doubling.
It equals about 0.02 mol, ignoring 2 NO₂ per Cu.
It equals 0.03 mol: no 3:1 ratio exists for NO₂ to Cu.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.3: molar volume is constant at a given temperature and pressure; the STP value is in the booklet.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books present 22.7 as a conversion alone. Exams chain it with an equation and a change of unit, and sometimes conditions that are not STP.

trap_boundaries: Molar volume applied at conditions where it does not hold (12M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
Dividing or multiplying by 2 despite a correct equation (12M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
Multi-step working: mass to moles to ratio, then molar volume of the given conditions (17M.2.SL.TZ1.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial attempts convert mass to moles but miss the equation ratio or the unit. Full credit needs all stages and the requested unit.

disguises: Excess reagent in a longer equation (25N.1A.HL.6207.26).
Gases only, no mass: limiting volume from the equation; 0.25 dm³ C₂H₂ with 0.40 dm³ H₂ gives 0.20 dm³ C₂H₆ (25N.1A.HL.6219.4).
Equal starting volumes with one gas left over (25N.1A.HL.6207.25).
Antacid CO₂ volume from a tablet mass (19M.3.SL.TZ1.16).
3_novel_application.heuristic: Is everything a gas at the same conditions? Use the ratio directly. Otherwise go through moles.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Written parts earn marks by stage; significant figures may be checked where stated (12M.2.HL.TZ2.2).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not use long routes through R when 22.7 applies, or assume STP when other conditions are given (24M.2.SL.TZ2.4).

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 2 gives 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ for STP only; section 4 defines STP as 273.15 K and 100 kPa and SATP as 298.15 K and 100 kPa. A molar volume at SATP is NOT in the booklet: use PV = nRT there.

rules: Map options to moles: at STP, 227 cm³ is 0.01 mol.
An option matching moles of the solid ignores any ratio other than 1:1.
Reject a dm³-sized number when cm³ is asked for.

evidence.note: Worked question, answer D.
Gas volumes and limiting reagent, answer A.
Equal gas volumes reacting, answer C.
Wrong factor of 2; wrong molar volume for the conditions; m³ not converted.
49.15% correct: mass to moles to molar volume.
Moles from a mass, then multiplied by the molar volume at the conditions given.
Over half calculated gas volume from a mass of carbonate.
Long-winded calculation assuming STP.

cards.difficulty_signal: Mid-range: 12M.1.SL.TZ2.3 at 49.15%; 'calculation of gas volume' flagged as difficult in the May 2024 report; appears twice in November 2025 Paper 1A.

cards.title: Sharp volume jump: think boiling, not gas laws

walkthrough.question: Propane is warmed at constant pressure from 200 K to 250 K, and its volume rises abruptly. A graph of straight-chain alkane boiling points places propane's boiling point between these two temperatures. Explain the abrupt rise in volume. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: A sharp volume jump signals boiling: gas particles are far further apart than liquid.
walkthrough.careful: State the change of state first; the second mark depends on it.
procedure: Compare the temperature range with the substance's boiling point.
Decide whether a change of state occurs.
State the change and that intermolecular forces are overcome.
Compare particle spacing in the two states.
tricks: Ratio check: 250/200 is only 25%, so gas expansion cannot be sharp.
Any sudden jump on heating: suspect state change. Fails if range misses boiling point.
if_lost: What state is propane in at 200 K?
Is the boiling point inside the range, and what does that mean?
How do particle separations compare in the two states?

1_context.short: Reads like a gas law question, but a state change decides.
1_context.why: Gas laws apply only once the sample is a gas. Between 200 K and 250 K the sample starts as liquid, so PV = nRT cannot describe the jump.
1_context.avoid: Answering with expansion and gas laws: most candidates did (24N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.2: real gases deviate from the ideal model, particularly at low temperature, where condensation can occur.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books treat the gas laws and states of matter in separate chapters. This question joins them through a boiling-point graph.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Boiling first; then gas molecules are further apart.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The mark for spacing or density is only awarded once a change of state is indicated, so naming the boiling comes first.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Only saying molecules spread out: M2 requires a change of state.
trigger_phrases: sufficient energy to overcome intermolecular forces
gaseous molecules further apart than in liquid
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: No M2 unless a change of state is indicated.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial: boils, with no spacing comparison. Full: boils, and gas far more spread out than liquid.

3_novel_application.short: The word 'sharply' is the clue, not the temperature values.
3_novel_application.why: A gas's volume rises only in proportion to kelvin temperature, so an abrupt change must come from something else: a change of state.
3_novel_application.avoid: Applying V ∝ T as soon as you see constant pressure.
3_novel_application.disguise: Constant pressure and heating look exactly like the temperature-volume relationship.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask whether the ratio of kelvin temperatures could account for the size of the change.

4_command_terms.short: Explain: give the cause and the reason, two linked points.
4_command_terms.why: Explain requires reasons, not just a description of the rise, and the two marks follow the chain from boiling to spacing.
4_command_terms.avoid: Restating that volume increases as temperature increases.
4_command_terms.demands: Give what happens to propane and why this raises the volume.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per point; M2 is conditional on a change of state being indicated.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two short sentences are enough for both marks.
5_time_efficiency.why: The marks reward two facts, so longer answers add risk of contradiction without gaining credit.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing out PV = nRT or calculating volumes.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip any calculation and gas-law statement: neither is on the markscheme.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet section helps; the graph gives the boiling range.
6_data_booklet.why: The evidence for boiling comes from the graph in the question, while the spacing idea is general knowledge of states.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for boiling points in the gas sections.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None: read the boiling point from the supplied graph.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: liquid and gas particle spacing, and that boiling overcomes intermolecular forces.

7_elimination.short: Expansion alone and bond breaking both score no credit here.
7_elimination.why: Neither names the state change: the first misses the cause, and the second confuses forces between molecules with bonds within them.
7_elimination.avoid: Writing 'particles move faster so gas expands'.

definitely_wrong.target: An answer about gas expanding on heating only
definitely_wrong.rule: It misses the change of state, the point most candidates lost.

definitely_wrong.target: An answer using PV = nRT proportionality
definitely_wrong.rule: 250/200 is only 25% more, which is not sharp.

definitely_wrong.target: An answer about breaking covalent bonds
definitely_wrong.rule: Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces; covalent bonds stay intact.

walkthrough.answer: M1: propane boils/vaporises, as molecules gain enough energy to overcome intermolecular forces. M2: gaseous molecules are much further apart than in the liquid (or gases are much less dense than liquids); M2 needs a change of state to be indicated.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.2: limitations of the ideal model, notably at low temperatures. Links to S1.5.4 as PV = nRT applies only to the gas.
1_context.textbook_gap: Textbooks seldom set a gas question in which the sample is not a gas. Exams use a boiling-point graph to test for that.

trap_boundaries: M2 only with a change of state indicated (24N.2.HL.TZ0.1).
Expansion and gas law answers miss the point (24N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
Liquid answers need the correct particle ideas: precision on 'volume of the container' was criticised (25M.2.SL.TZ3.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Mean 0.54/2 in HL. The difference between 0 and 2 is usually whether the state change was noticed.

disguises: Sharp volume change on heating at constant pressure (24N.2.HL.TZ0.1).
Graphs of particle behaviour: relating data to the sub-microscopic was flagged in May 2018 reports.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Before any gas law, ask: is the sample a gas at both temperatures?

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Per-point marks with a dependency: M2 is conditional on M1's state change.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No calculation is needed for 2 marks, so write two sentences and move on.

6_data_booklet.hack: No booklet help in the gas sections. Particle spacing in states is NOT in the booklet: memorise it. Use the question's own graph.

rules: A gas law statement alone fails if the sample changes state in the range.
Any mention of covalent bonds breaking on boiling is wrong for molecular substances.

evidence.note: Boils; molecules further apart; M2 only with change of state. Mean 0.54/2.
Most missed the state change and only cited expansion; about 20% earned credit.
Links between macroscopic liquid properties and particles were weak.

cards.difficulty_signal: Mean 0.54/2 at HL and about 20% credit at SL in November 2024, despite being described as reachable: high value because the trap is single and avoidable.

cards.title: Boiling means intermolecular forces, never covalent bonds

walkthrough.question: Methane, ethane and propane are all gases at room temperature, yet their boiling points climb in that order. Explain this trend. [2]
walkthrough.key_idea: Boiling overcomes London forces, which strengthen with more electrons; covalent bonds stay intact.
walkthrough.careful: Name the force; never write about breaking covalent bonds.
procedure: Identify the intermolecular forces between the molecules.
Say how their strength changes across the series.
Link that change to electrons or molecular size.
Relate stronger forces to the higher boiling point.
tricks: Alkane means London forces only. Fails once a polar group is present.
Write 'between molecules' to prevent any hint of bond breaking.
if_lost: What is actually separated when a liquid boils?
Which intermolecular force acts between non-polar molecules?
What changes about the electrons from methane to propane?

1_context.short: Real gases have forces; boiling points show their strength.
1_context.why: The ideal model assumes no intermolecular forces. A gas that can liquefy must have them, and stronger forces mean a higher boiling point.
1_context.avoid: Treating boiling as chemical change inside molecules.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.1: ideal gases have no intermolecular forces, unlike the real alkanes here.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books treat forces under bonding. This question places them in a gas context and marks the type of force and its trend.

2_markscheme_logic.short: London forces first; strength grows with electrons or size.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Two separate facts each earn a mark: the type of force, and the reason its strength increases along the series.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Saying propane has more bonds to break: reported in 24N.2.SL.TZ0.1.
trigger_phrases: size of electron cloud / number of electrons
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Mass or size is accepted for M2 only tied to intermolecular force strength.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One mark names the force or the trend. Two marks give the force and why it strengthens.

3_novel_application.short: It sits inside a gas question, but tests forces.
3_novel_application.why: A gas context pushes you to think about gas laws, yet boiling-point trends always depend on what holds the liquid together.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using molecular speed or gas laws to explain boiling points.
3_novel_application.disguise: A question about gases at room temperature hides a question about the liquid state.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Boiling-point question: ask what holds the liquid's particles together.

4_command_terms.short: Explain: name the force and give why it strengthens.
4_command_terms.why: Explain demands a cause. Stating that bigger molecules boil higher only restates the pattern, not the reason.
4_command_terms.avoid: Describing the trend without naming a force.
4_command_terms.demands: Give the force type and the reason for its increasing strength.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Two marks, one per point; mean was 1.27/2 at HL.

5_time_efficiency.short: One sentence on the force, one on its trend.
5_time_efficiency.why: The marks match two facts, so two sentences secure them, and any extra statement risks a contradiction.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Discussing hydrogen bonding and dipoles to be safe.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip other force types and any mention of covalent bonds.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet section helps; this is pure structure reasoning.
6_data_booklet.why: Force types and their trends are not given in the sections listed for this topic, so this reasoning must come from memory.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for boiling points.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None: reason from the molecule's electrons and size.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NOT in the booklet: London forces act between non-polar molecules and strengthen with more electrons.

7_elimination.short: Covalent bond and hydrogen bond answers are out instantly.
7_elimination.why: Boiling leaves covalent bonds intact, and alkanes have no H on N, O or F, so neither explanation can apply.
7_elimination.avoid: Adding dipole-dipole forces to appear thorough.

definitely_wrong.target: An answer about breaking C–H or C–C bonds

definitely_wrong.rule: Alkanes have no H bonded to N, O or F.

walkthrough.answer: M1: only London (dispersion) forces act between the molecules. M2: these forces strengthen as the electron cloud/number of electrons increases. Accept strength rising with mass or size of molecule for M2.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S1.5.1 and S1.5.2: the ideal model ignores intermolecular forces, whereas real gases have them and can liquefy.
1_context.textbook_gap: Forces are taught under bonding, but examiners expect them to be used in gas contexts, and the bond-breaking misconception persists.

trigger_phrases: increases with electron cloud size or number of electrons
trap_boundaries: Boiling described as breaking intramolecular covalent bonds is a known misconception (24N.2.HL.TZ0.1).
'More bonds to break' earns nothing for this trend (24N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
Forces must be compared, not merely listed (24M.2.SL.TZ2.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Mean 1.27/2 at HL: most got the size idea; full marks also name London forces.

disguises: Boiling-point graph inside a gas question (24N.2.HL.TZ0.1).
3_novel_application.heuristic: If molecules stay intact, only forces between them can be involved.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per point. Comparing forces needs reference to both substances (24M.2.SL.TZ2.4).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not list every force type: alkanes need London forces only.

6_data_booklet.hack: No booklet support in the gas sections. Force types and trends are NOT in the booklet: memorise them.

rules: Any boiling explanation with covalent bonds breaking is wrong for molecular substances.
Hydrogen bonding needs H on N, O or F, so it is wrong for alkanes.

evidence.note: London forces; strength with electron cloud; size accepted. Mean 1.27/2; bond-breaking misconception.
About 40% understood; many said propane has more bonds to break.
Candidates did not compare the forces in each compound.
LDF exists between all molecules; misunderstanding in volatility comparison.
Forces compared to explain differing gas behaviour.

cards.difficulty_signal: Mean 1.27/2 at HL and a strong discriminator; easier than the unit traps, but the same misconception recurs in several reports.

cross_links.note: Moles from mass (n = m/M) is the first stage of nearly every gas calculation.
Reacting gas volumes and limiting gases (25N.1A.HL.6219.4, 25N.1A.HL.6207.25) use mole ratios directly; the full method belongs there.
London forces and hydrogen bonding explain which real gases deviate most and why boiling points rise.
